title: Why "think step by step" works on AI

Each step it writes goes back in before it answers.
Newer reasoning models do the steps on their own. Do you still need them? Yes or no.

youtube_title: Why "Think Step by Step" Works on AI 🤔
youtube_title_alternatives: Five Words That Helped AI Do Math 🤔
The Puzzle a 2022 AI Got Wrong 🤔
youtube_description:
Five words: "Let's think step by step." Why does that help AI?

In a 2022 paper from the University of Tokyo and Google, Kojima et al. showed that large language models "are decent zero-shot reasoners by simply adding "Let's think step by step" before each answer." With one 2022 model (InstructGPT, text-davinci-002, a GPT-3 series model), accuracy on the MultiArith math word problems went "from 17.7% to 78.7%".

Try the paper's own puzzle: 16 balls, half are golf balls, half of the golf balls are blue. How many blue golf balls? Asked straight, the model said 8. With the five words, it wrote the steps first (16 balls, 8 golf balls, 4 blue) and then answered 4.

Why it works: a chatbot guesses its answer from the text in front of it. In the paper's method, the steps the model writes are fed back in with the question before the answer is asked for. The paper calls that prompt "self-augmented, since the prompt contains the sentence z generated by the same language model." So the answer is guessed with those steps in view.

Order matters. In a separate 2022 paper, Wei et al. (Google) tested steps written only after the answer. That version "performs about the same as the baseline", meaning no steps at all.

Newer reasoning models do the steps on their own. OpenAI's reasoning guide says: "Since these models perform reasoning internally, prompting them to "think step by step" or "explain your reasoning" is unnecessary." A 2025 Wharton report found that for models built to reason, chain-of-thought prompting "often results in only marginal, if any, gains in answer accuracy."

So, do you still need them? Yes or no.

Fine print: the voice rounds 17.7% and 78.7% to 18 and 79; the screen shows the exact figures. Both numbers are one model (text-davinci-002, run through OpenAI's API in April and May 2022) on one test (MultiArith); the same paper found on-par results on two easier math tests, no gains on its commonsense tests, and that step-by-step reasoning "is not effective" on smaller models. The puzzle is the paper's Figure 1, shortened (the juggler is dropped); today's chatbots are not shown answering it. The "steps after the answer" beat is our illustration of Wei et al., who tested LaMDA 137B and PaLM 540B on GSM8K, not this puzzle. "Guesses its answer" is our plain wording for the paper's answer step. The chat box, answer strip, paper card and guide card are hand-made re-creations; no real app or logo is shown. OpenAI's guide is about OpenAI's own reasoning models.

Sources:
- Kojima, Gu, Reid, Matsuo, Iwasawa, "Large Language Models are Zero-Shot Reasoners", arXiv 2205.11916, submitted May 24, 2022 (NeurIPS 2022), read Nov 2, 2026: https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.11916
- Wei et al. (Google Research), "Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models", arXiv 2201.11903, submitted Jan 28, 2022, section 3.3, read Nov 2, 2026: https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.11903
- OpenAI, "Reasoning best practices" (developer guide), read Nov 2, 2026: https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/reasoning-best-practices
- Meincke, Mollick, Mollick, Shapiro (Wharton Generative AI Labs), "Prompting Science Report 2: The Decreasing Value of Chain of Thought in Prompting", arXiv 2506.07142, June 8, 2025, read Nov 2, 2026: https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.07142
